title: AI Adoption in Corporate Legal Departments Doubles According to The General Counsel Report
author: FTI Consulting · Relativity

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The supplied source evidence covers only research methodology and organizational descriptions of FTI Consulting and Relativity. It provides no substantive findings or arguments on jagged AI capability, selective deployment, human verification, or operating-model redesign, so its position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source accepts and materially strengthens the cluster’s account of corporate legal departments as a principal catalyst for AI-driven change. It adds survey evidence of sharply increased in-house adoption and formal technology planning, while its emphasis on structured training, expert support and risk-aware roadmaps reinforces organisational absorption as the key implementation requirement. It does not establish realised cost savings, insourcing or market-wide pricing effects.
qs: (NYSE: FCN) and legal data intelligence company Relativity, show generative artificial intelligence (“AI”) adoption in corporate legal departments has nearly doubled year over year, with 87% of general counsel now reporting use within their teams, compared with 44% in 2025.
Legal departments that have a formalized technology roadmap in place also reached an all-time high of 53%, more than double from 25% the previous year.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster with large-organisation, buyer-side evidence that generative AI is being mainstreamed chiefly in bounded, document-oriented workflows. Its call for structured training, expert support and risk-aware technology roadmaps reinforces the cluster’s emphasis on user capability and organisational complements, though it does not independently establish productivity gains, verification burdens or competence loss.
qs: When asked about their comfort with generative AI use for certain tasks, respondents expressed the most openness for legal research, e-discovery, document review, contract drafting and contract analysis.

kp.k: Reported in-house generative AI adoption nearly doubles
kp.d: The March 11, 2026 release from FTI Consulting and Relativity reports that 87% of general counsel now report generative AI use within their teams, compared with 44% in 2025. This is a reported adoption finding about corporate legal departments, rather than a measure of productivity or replacement of lawyers.
qs: generative artificial intelligence (“AI”) adoption in corporate legal departments has nearly doubled year over year, with 87% of general counsel now reporting use within their teams, compared with 44% in 2025.

kp.k: Technology roadmaps and planned investment expand
kp.d: The report finds that 39% view AI as a strategic priority for legal department efficiency and efficacy. Formalized technology roadmaps reached a reported all-time high of 53%, up from 25% the previous year, while approximately 70% plan new technology investment in the next 12 months. These investment plans concern technology generally, not solely AI.
qs: 39% now view AI as among their strategic priorities for supporting legal department efficiency and efficacy.
Legal departments that have a formalized technology roadmap in place also reached an all-time high of 53%, more than double from 25% the previous year.
approximately 70% plan to invest in new technologies in the next 12 months

kp.k: Summarization leads reported use and experimentation
kp.d: Respondents expressed greatest openness to generative AI for legal research, e-discovery, document review, contract drafting and contract analysis. Summarization led reported use or experimentation at 83%, followed by identifying contract clauses (63%), audio and video transcription (53%), foreign-language material analysis (40%) and first-pass review (37%). The figures combine use and experimentation rather than establishing routine deployment for every task.
qs: When asked about their comfort with generative AI use for certain tasks, respondents expressed the most openness for legal research, e-discovery, document review, contract drafting and contract analysis.
Respondents said the most common task for generative AI was summarization, with 83% either using or experimenting with it.
This was followed by identifying contract clauses (63%), audio and video transcription (53%), analysis of foreign language materials (40%) and first-pass review (37%).

kp.k: Ross recommends structured upskilling and risk-conscious technology planning
kp.d: FTI Technology's Sophie Ross asserts that most legal departments not yet using generative AI plan near-term implementation. She recommends structured training, education and expert support as in-house teams become comfortable with more use cases, supported by technology roadmaps that combine innovation with risk mitigation. These are her forward-looking claims and recommendations.
qs: Generative AI has become a fixture in the majority of legal departments, and of those not yet using it, most have plans to implement in the near term
As in-house teams grow more comfortable with a wide range of generative AI use cases, appropriate upskilling will be imperative.

General counsel will need to provide their departments with structured training, education and expert support to use this technology effectively, and underpin those efforts with technology roadmaps that enable innovation alongside risk mitigation.

kp.k: Horrigan interprets adoption as a professional identity shift
kp.d: Relativity's David Horrigan interprets the report as evidence of a shift from the 'Luddite Lawyer' to the 'TechnoLawyer.' He cites chief legal officers' generative AI use rising from 20% in 2023 to 87% in this year's report and reports that participating chief information officers see 'digital ambassadors' emerging within legal departments. The professional-identity framing is his interpretation of the reported adoption trend and technical leaders' commentary.
qs: For instance, the report shows that chief legal officers’ use of generative AI has steadily and substantially increased, from a mere 20% using generative AI in 2023 to 87% in this year’s report.

In addition, with chief information officers included in this year’s report expressing that they see ‘digital ambassadors’ emerging in legal departments, it’s clear we’re entering a new era of the ‘TechnoLawyer.’

kp.k: Evidence combines 2025 interviews and large-organization survey responses
kp.d: Although released as the 2026 report, the described fieldwork occurred in 2025. Ari Kaplan interviewed 30 general counsel or chief legal officers in September 2025; 63% had global responsibilities and 59% worked in organizations exceeding $500 million annual revenue. Separately, Censuswide surveyed 224 general counsel and chief legal officers in summer 2025 at organizations exceeding $100 million annual revenue and 1,000 employees across South America, North America, Europe and Asia Pacific. Technical and transformation leaders supplied anecdotal perspectives on their overlap with general counsel, included for the first time this year.
qs: In September 2025, Ari Kaplan conducted personal interviews with 30 leaders serving as general counsel or chief legal officers of their organizations.
Sixty-three percent have a role with global responsibilities and 59% work in organizations with more than $500 million in annual revenue.
He also interviewed technology and digital transformation leaders at global organizations for anecdotal insights into how their responsibilities and views overlap with the general counsel.

Separately, in the summer of 2025, Censuswide conducted a quantitative survey of 224 general counsel and chief legal officers at organizations with more than $100 million in annual revenue and more than 1,000 employees in South America, North America, Europe and Asia Pacific.

For the first time, this year’s findings include insights from c-level technical leaders, including chief information officers and heads of transformation within large organizations, providing commentary on the dynamics between legal department leaders and their cross-department counterparts.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: FTI Consulting and Relativity report that generative AI adoption has nearly doubled in corporate legal departments and is becoming a strategic priority.
pts.d: The release reports that 87% of general counsel say their teams use generative AI, compared with 44% in the 2025 report, and that 39% consider AI a strategic priority for departmental efficiency and efficacy. It also reports growing technology planning and intended investment: 53% have formal technology roadmaps, up from 25%, and approximately 70% plan new technology investments. The roadmap and investment figures concern technology generally, not exclusively AI; efficiency and efficacy are stated strategic objectives rather than measured outcomes.

pts.k: The release identifies summarization as the leading generative AI application and reports adoption or experimentation across document, contract and review tasks.
pts.d: Respondents most commonly reported using or experimenting with summarization (83%), followed by identifying contract clauses (63%), audio and video transcription (53%), analysis of foreign-language materials (40%) and first-pass review (37%). Respondents expressed the greatest comfort with legal research, e-discovery, document review, contract drafting and contract analysis. These findings describe task use, experimentation and openness, rather than demonstrated performance improvements or autonomous replacement of lawyers.

pts.k: Sophie Ross says AI is now a fixture in most legal departments and predicts that broader use will make structured upskilling imperative.
pts.d: Ross, Global Chief Executive Officer of FTI Technology, says most departments not yet using generative AI plan near-term implementation. She argues that effective use will require general counsel to provide training, education and expert support, backed by technology roadmaps combining innovation with risk mitigation. This is a forward-looking management prescription accompanying the adoption findings.

pts.k: David Horrigan interprets rising AI adoption and emerging legal-department digital ambassadors as a shift toward a technology-oriented general counsel role.
pts.d: Horrigan, Relativity’s Discovery Counsel and Legal Education Director, characterizes the findings as the end of the 'Luddite Lawyer' and the emergence of the 'TechnoLawyer.' He bases this interpretation on a reported increase in chief legal officers’ generative AI use from 20% in 2023 to 87% in the current report, together with chief information officers’ observations of digital ambassadors in legal departments. These labels are his interpretation of the reported changes, not separate quantitative findings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims draw on executive interviews, a separate 224-person survey and comparisons with earlier report editions; technology-leader commentary supplies anecdotal evidence.
pts.d: Ari Kaplan interviewed 30 general counsel or chief legal officers in September 2025; 63% had global responsibilities and 59% worked at organizations with annual revenue above $500 million. Censuswide separately surveyed 224 general counsel and chief legal officers in summer 2025 at organizations with revenue above $100 million and more than 1,000 employees. The release describes coverage across a dozen countries and four regions. It also includes interviews with technology and transformation leaders, explicitly described as anecdotal insights. The release does not assign each reported percentage to a particular data pool or provide prior-edition sampling details. Ross’s upskilling prescription and Horrigan’s professional-change interpretation accompany these findings; no measured training effects or task-performance benchmarks are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The March 2026 release reports findings collected in 2025, compares report editions and presents near-term implementation and investment intentions.
pts.d: Published March 11, 2026, the release describes summer and September 2025 fieldwork. Its 87% adoption figure is framed as the current or 2026 report finding, compared with 44% in the 2025 report; Horrigan extends the comparison to 20% in 2023. Technology investment intentions cover the next 12 months, without specifying whether that period is anchored to fieldwork or publication. Ross describes remaining adoption plans as near term without a precise deadline. Her claim about effective use is conditional on structured training, education, expert support and roadmaps that address risk. Task figures include experimentation and therefore do not uniformly represent established production use.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected group is corporate in-house legal teams, especially those in large organizations, alongside their general counsel and technology-leadership counterparts.
pts.d: The findings concern the buyer side of legal services: corporate legal departments and their GC/CLO leaders. Team members are reported to be using or testing AI for research, discovery, document processing and contract work, while leaders face technology-planning, investment and training responsibilities. CIOs and transformation leaders contribute observations about cross-department relationships and emerging digital ambassadors. The quantitative sample consists of large employers across South America, North America, Europe and Asia Pacific. The release does not make concrete claims about law-firm staffing, ALSP market share, lawyer displacement, legal fees or changes in the public’s access to justice.
